definition.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time.

facts.text: By lowering the carbon dioxide in the air it helps manage the carbon cycle and limit climate change.
The two main types are biologic sequestration, also called biosequestration, and geologic sequestration.
Plants take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow and bind it into biomass; people can speed this up through land use and farming.
Biological stores such as forests may be temporary, since fires, disease, economic pressure and politics can release the carbon.
Injecting CO2 underground or turning it into carbonate salts locks carbon away for thousands to millions of years.
Within carbon capture and storage, sequestration is the storage step.
A 2025 study found that using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C.

title: Biological carbon sequestration
article: Carbon sequestration#Biological carbon sequestration on land

definition.text: Capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide through living processes, mainly plant growth, that people keep up and enhance.

facts.text: It works by raising photosynthesis through land uses such as reforestation and sustainable forest management.
Forests act as land carbon sinks, storing carbon in roots, stems, branches and leaves.
Converting natural land to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30–40%.
Wetlands hold 20–30% of the world's soil carbon on only 5–8% of its land.

title: Geological carbon sequestration
article: Carbon sequestration#Underground storage in suitable geologic formations

definition.text: Storing carbon dioxide deep underground in depleted oil and gas fields, saline formations or coal beds that cannot be mined.

facts.text: Captured CO2 is compressed to about 100 bar, piped to the site and injected around 1 km deep, where it can stay for hundreds to millions of years.
A good site has porous, permeable rock such as sandstone under a tight cap rock such as shale.
Risks include CO2 leaking up along faults and earthquakes caused by too much pressure.
2025 research found that of nearly 12,000 GtCO2 of theoretical storage capacity, only 1,460 GtCO2 is risk-free.
Storage alone, without capture and transport, can cost below US$10 per tonne where onshore storage is available.

definition.text: Locking carbon dioxide into solid carbonate minerals by reacting it with metal oxides such as magnesium or calcium oxide.

facts.text: The same reaction happens slowly in nature and built up much of Earth's limestone over geologic time.
It can be sped up with heat, pressure, catalysts or by grinding minerals, but this needs extra energy.
CO2 dissolved in water and injected into hot basalt underground turns into solid carbonate minerals.

definition.text: Storing carbon by burying wood or other plant matter where it cannot rot, mimicking how fossil fuels formed.

facts.text: Its global potential is estimated at 10 ± 5 GtC per year, highest in tropical forests.
A 2008 estimate put wood burial costs at US$50 per tonne of carbon, much cheaper than capturing power-plant emissions.

title: Direct deep-sea CO2 injection
article: Carbon sequestration#Direct deep-sea carbon dioxide injection

definition.text: An abandoned idea of storing carbon dioxide by injecting it directly into the deep ocean for some centuries.

facts.text: Interest fell after about 2001 because of unknown effects on marine life, high costs and doubts about how long the carbon would stay.
The IPCC listed it in 2005 but no longer mentioned ocean storage in 2014.
